To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optically thin, stellar wind from the compact components in symbiotic systems is the dominant source of broad H wings during active and quiescent phases, with mass-loss rates of a few 108 M yr 1 in the former and a few (107 106) M yr 1in the latter.

the broad H wings observed during active phases in symbiotic binaries are formed in the optically thin, ionized stellar wind of the hotter components and the mass-loss rates of these components are of a magnitude similar to those of the classical hot post-AGB stars.

we have found that broad H wings in the spectra of symbiotic binaries can be modeled very well by an optically-thin, bipolar stellar wind of the central hot component and the mass-loss rates from these stars are in the order of 10 8 10 7 M yr 1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optically thin, ionized stellar wind model of the hot components of symbiotic binaries as the source of the observed broad wings of the Balmer lines.
the modeling and interpretation of the broad H wings in a sample of 10 Symbiotics.
the optically thin, ionized stellar wind as an alternative to the Raman-scattering mechanism to explain the broad H wings observed from symbiotic binaries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the broad H wings in symbiotic stars are formed by both the Raman scattering as well as the stellar wind from the central hot component.
both processes, i.e., Raman scattering and the stellar wind, contribute to the formation of broad H wings.
the H wings are a superposition of both the Raman scattering and the ionized stellar winds from the hot components.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the H wings observed in the symbiotic stars during their active phase are formed in the optically thin, ionized stellar wind of their hot components, while those observed in quiescent phase are formed in a combination of the optically thin wind and the Raman scattering on atomic hydrogen.
the broad H wings observed during active phases in symbiotic binaries can be explained as arising from the optically-thin stellar wind from the central hot component.
the H wings in the symbiotic stars can be explained by the stellar wind model as well as by the Raman scattering model and that the stellar wind model is preferred during active phases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the optically thin, ionized, bipolar stellar wind can be an alternative to the Raman-scattered Ly line as the source of the broad H wings in symbiotic binaries, which are often observed during active phases.
the optically thin wind model is able to account for the observed broad H -emission in a large fraction of symbiotics, and therefore it is an alternative to the Raman scattering model.
a stellar wind can be an alternative source to Raman scattering to account for broad H wings.
